items.title: Gentrification displaces existing residents through rising rents
items.claim: What is the mechanism of gentrification?

options.text: A purely positive process with no losers

Wealthier newcomers move into a previously disinvested neighbourhood; property prices and rents rise; existing lower-income residents (often disproportionately ethnic minority) are displaced — Neil Smith's 'rent gap' theory (1979) explains the economic mechanism
State demolition of all old housing

items.reveal:
Ruth Glass coined 'gentrification' in 1964 in 'London: Aspects of Change', describing the takeover of Islington working-class housing by middle-class incomers. Neil Smith's 'rent gap' theory (1979) explained the economic incentive: the gap between actual rent under disinvestment and potential rent after re-investment attracts capital.

London examples: Notting Hill (1960s onwards), Brixton (2000s), Hackney (2000s-2010s). Berlin: Prenzlauer Berg, Kreuzberg. New York: SoHo, Williamsburg.

Mitigation policies — affordable housing quotas, right-to-return clauses on estate redevelopment, rent control — have variable effectiveness. Sharon Zukin and others have argued the cultural displacement (loss of community) is as significant as the housing displacement.
items.why: Urban regeneration produces winners and losers. 'Rejuvenation' narratives obscure who is being displaced and who the city is being improved for — central to contemporary urban geography.

items.title: El Nino and La Nina drive global climate every 2-7 years
items.claim: What is the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)?

options.text: A single storm in the Pacific
A coupled ocean-atmosphere oscillation in the tropical Pacific that occurs every 2-7 years; El Nino (warm phase) and La Nina (cool phase) reshape global rainfall, drought and storm patterns
An annual cycle in the Arctic

items.reveal:
El Nino: warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, weakened trade winds, shifted convection. Effects include drought in Australia, Indonesia and South Africa; floods in Peru, Ecuador and east Africa; weaker Atlantic hurricane season.

La Nina: opposite phase. The 1997-98 El Nino was among the strongest; 2015-16 caused mass coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef and contributed to record global temperatures.

Gilbert Walker first identified the 'Southern Oscillation' atmospheric pattern in 1924 from Indian Meteorological Department records.
items.why: Global weather is partly oscillatory. Forecasts months ahead become more skilful when ENSO state is known — and crops, water supplies and disaster planning in many countries depend on the call.

items.title: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean
items.claim: What does standard deviation tell you?

options.text: The highest value in the data
The typical (root mean square) deviation from the mean — about 68% of normally distributed data lies within one SD of the mean, 95% within two SD, 99.7% within three SD

items.reveal:
Standard deviation σ is calculated as the square root of the average squared deviation from the mean. For a normal distribution, the 68-95-99.7 rule applies — though many geographical datasets are not normal (skewed by extremes).

In fieldwork: comparing pebble sizes on two beaches, two questionnaire response distributions, or rainfall variability at two stations. A small SD means data cluster near the mean; a large SD means high variability.

Coefficient of variation (CV = SD/mean) allows comparison between datasets with different means — useful when comparing variability across scales.
items.why: Statistical literacy underpins geographical analysis. Reporting only a mean hides whether the data are tightly clustered or wildly variable — and the difference often matters more than the mean itself.
